event: Genoese ships from Caffa bring plague to Messina, Sicily. Rats and fleas carry the disease ashore. Europe's worst disaster begins.
The Black Death reaches Florence. Within months, half the population is dead. Bodies are piled in the streets. The living cannot bury the dead fast enough.
The plague reaches Avignon, seat of the papacy. Pope Clement VI consecrates the Rhône river so bodies can be thrown in — the cemeteries are full.
Marseille is devastated by the plague. The port city that received the disease from Italian ships loses half its people in weeks.
The plague spreads north through France, reaches England, Germany, and Scandinavia. A third of Europe's population will die within three years.
The plague returns in a second wave, killing many who survived the first. Children born since 1348 are especially vulnerable.
Flagellant processions march through Italian and French cities. Penitents whip themselves bloody in the streets, believing the plague is God's punishment for human sin.
Pogroms against Jews across Germany and France. Accused of poisoning wells to cause the plague, thousands are massacred in Strasbourg, Basel, and Mainz.
Pope Clement VI issues a papal bull defending the Jews and condemning the pogroms. He declares the plague is not their fault. Few listen.
The great Florentine banking houses of the Bardi and Peruzzi collapse after King Edward III of England defaults on massive war loans. Florence's economy is shattered.
Trade across Europe collapses as cities close their gates against the plague. Merchants cannot sell goods. Ships sit empty in harbors. The economy stops.
Labor is suddenly scarce after the plague. Surviving peasants demand higher wages. Landowners are furious but have no choice. The old feudal order begins to crack.
The Hundred Years War begins as Edward III of England claims the French throne. England and France will fight for over a century.
Battle of Crécy — English longbowmen slaughter French knights. The mounted charge that defined medieval warfare is rendered obsolete.
Battle of Poitiers — the French king John II is captured by the English. France descends into chaos. The Estates-General demands reforms.
Food rots in the fields around Siena. There are not enough living people to harvest the crops. Bread is available but no one can bring it to market.
Boccaccio begins writing the Decameron — stories told by young Florentines who fled the plague to a villa in the countryside. Literature born from catastrophe.
A series of bad harvests across northern Italy and southern France. Food prices rise sharply. The poor are already weakened when the plague arrives.
Siena's government collapses. Half the city council is dead from the plague. The survivors cannot maintain order. Looting begins in the empty quarters.
Florence slowly rebuilds after the plague. Wages for laborers have doubled. Skilled craftsmen can name their price. The survivors inherit the wealth of the dead.
